q: Live plants could not survive a long sea voyage until a sealed glazed case was devised in the 1830s, and within a few decades three American vine diseases had crossed to Europe. What was that case called?
exp: It is a closed box of glass in which a plant recycles its own moisture, and it transformed the movement of plants around the empires of the nineteenth century. Faster steamships did the rest: a pest that starved on a six-week crossing arrived alive on a two-week one.

q: Hundreds of thousands of growers marched through the towns of the French Midi in the summer of 1907, and a regiment sent to keep order mutinied and joined them. What had brought them out?
opts: A new land tax on every planted hectare in the south
An order requiring every vine to be grafted
Fraudulent wine had collapsed the price of their own
The closure of their main export route
exp: Sugared and watered wine, together with cheap imports from across the Mediterranean, had flooded the market just as the vineyard recovered from the louse. The state answered with laws against fraud and with the first obligation on growers to declare their harvest, which is the ancestor of every modern production record.

q: A single-issue pressure group worked seat by seat through American state legislatures, backing any candidate who would vote dry and punishing any who would not. Which group did most to write national prohibition into the constitution?
exp: Endorsing dry candidates of either party, and never running its own, made it the model for modern single-issue lobbying. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union had been building the moral case since 1874, close to half a century by the time the ban passed, but the legislative machinery belonged to the league.

q: The constitutional ban needed a statute to say what counted as an intoxicating drink, and the statute drew the line at half of one percent alcohol. What is that statute called?
exp: Half a percent catches ordinary beer and cider comfortably, which is why so much of the trade closed rather than trying to reformulate around it. The same figure survives in American law as the threshold below which a drink may be sold as non-alcoholic.

q: Repeal came in 1933, and it had to be done the way the ban had been imposed, by amending the constitution a second time. Which amendment repealed it?
exp: The Eighteenth had imposed prohibition, and the Twenty-first is the only amendment ever passed purely to undo another one. It handed control of alcohol back to the individual states, which is why drinks law in the United States still changes sharply at a state line.

q: A tiny French crop, cut back by a hard spring frost and then ripened through a hot dry summer, was picked in the year the war in Europe ended. Which vintage is still spoken of as one of the century's greatest?
exp: Frost in May reduced the crop to a fraction of a normal year, and what survived was small-berried, thick-skinned and concentrated. Bottles from that harvest were still showing well half a century later, which is how a year becomes a byword rather than merely a good vintage.

q: An intergovernmental body founded in Paris in 1924 gathers the world's vineyard and harvest statistics and writes the technical standards that national wine laws borrow from. Which body?
opts: The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations
exp: Its name in full is the International Organisation of Vine and Wine, and it grew out of the same fraud crisis that forced countries to agree what words like wine and vineyard actually meant. Its analytical methods and category definitions are written into the law of many countries that are not even members.

q: Burgundian growers sold their wine in cask to merchants until the 1930s, when a French wine writer and an American importer began persuading them to do something else. What was it?
opts: Sell only through the local cooperative
Bottle their own wine at the property
Sell their grapes rather than their wine
Blend across several villages before selling
exp: The pair were hunting for wine that tasted of one particular place, and concluded that the only way to keep it that way was to have it bottled where it was made. Growers became names in their own right as a result, and the modern market in single-grower Burgundy dates from that decade.

q: A London examining body set up by the wine trade in 1955 awards a qualification whose holders may put two letters after their names. Which body is it?
opts: The Wine and Spirit Education Trust
The Institute of Masters of Wine
exp: Its examination covers theory, blind tasting and a research paper, and it was opened beyond the British trade in the 1980s. It is an examining institute rather than a trade association, which is much of why the qualification travels as well as it does.

q: An examining body formally established in London in 1977 tests candidates on restaurant service and salesmanship as well as on blind tasting and theory. Which is it?
opts: The Institute of Masters of Wine
exp: Its examination is built around what actually happens at the table, under the clock, in front of a guest. That focus is what separates it from the trade and production qualifications, and it is why its title is the one used on a restaurant floor.

q: Two flights were poured at the 1976 Paris tasting, one red and one white, and each set Californian bottles against French ones made from the same principal grape. Which pair of grapes was used?
exp: The reds went up against classed-growth Bordeaux and the whites against white Burgundy, so both flights were chosen where California was working with the same varieties as the benchmark. That choice is why the outcome was read as a like-for-like comparison rather than a curiosity.

q: The reds from the 1976 Paris line-up were opened again thirty years later, on the widely held assumption that the Californian bottles would long since have collapsed. What happened?
opts: The judges declared the result a tie
The Bordeaux took the top five places
exp: They had aged perfectly well, and a Californian red again topped the ranking. The original result had been dismissed on the grounds that the French wines were built to last and the Californians were not, and the re-tasting removed that objection.

q: An American lawyer began publishing an independent newsletter on wine in 1978, scoring bottles out of a hundred and refusing all advertising, and buying habits worldwide followed his numbers for a generation. Who was he?
exp: Taking no advertising was the whole point, because it meant readers could believe that nobody in the trade had paid for the verdict. A single number is easy to print on a shelf label and easy to trade on, which is why the scale spread far beyond the publication that introduced it.

q: Wine is produced commercially in every Italian administrative region. How many such regions does the country have?
exp: All twenty regions grow grapes for sale, from Alpine Valle d'Aosta to Sicily. Very few wine countries can say the same, and it is part of why the native grape count is so high.

q: Italy's two main wine-producing islands lie off the west and the south. Which are they?
exp: Sicily sits off the toe of the peninsula and Sardinia west of the mainland. Both have long, hot seasons tempered by sea breezes and by planting at altitude.

q: Bardolino and Lugana are grown beside which large lake?
exp: Garda's mass of water warms and cools slowly, damping temperature extremes on its shores. The lighter reds and whites grown around it depend on that moderation.
